analogy.p: A chef (the CPU) follows a recipe card (the program). The **bookmark** showing which line to read next is the **PC**. The chef reads the line at the bookmark (**fetch**), works out what it means, for example 'chop the onions' (**decode**), and does it (**execute**), then moves the bookmark on one line and repeats. The chef's **notepad** for the running total is the **accumulator**. The analogy breaks down because a chef reads words in English and can look ahead, whereas the CPU follows binary machine code and in the simple model handles one instruction at a time, billions of times faster than any person.
analogy.t: A chef following a numbered recipe

bullets: Name the three stages in order: **fetch, then decode, then execute**, then the cycle **repeats**.
State the job of each register: **PC, MAR, MDR, ACC** (and know the **current instruction register, CIR**, appears in many textbooks).
Say what the **control unit (CU)** does (decodes, controls, sends control signals) and what the **ALU** does (arithmetic and logic).
Know that the cycle is repeated **billions of times per second**, controlled by the **clock**.
Know where each step happens: registers and CU inside the CPU, instructions in **RAM**.
Be able to follow a short **trace** showing register values changing.
Be able to link the cycle to performance (clock speed, cache, cores).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: OCR J277 1.1 requires you to know the **Von Neumann architecture** and the **fetch-decode-execute cycle**: how the CPU repeatedly fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it and executes it, and what the registers (**Program Counter, Memory Address Register, Memory Data Register and Accumulator**), the **control unit** and the **ALU** do at each stage. You are expected to **describe the stages in the correct order**, say which register holds what, and say which bus carries what. It matters because this is the core mechanism of every computer, and it is a regular source of 3 to 6 mark questions where precise ordering and vocabulary decide the marks.

bullets: **Fetch**: get the next instruction from memory.
**Decode**: work out what the instruction is asking the CPU to do.
**Execute**: carry out the instruction.
The cycle is **repeated for every instruction** in the program until the program ends.
A modern CPU performs this process **billions of times per second** (a 3 GHz CPU has 3 billion clock cycles per second).
It uses the **Von Neumann stored program** idea: the instructions are in RAM as binary, just like data.
Only one stage of the **simple model** happens at a time in a single core; real CPUs overlap stages for speed, but GCSE uses the simple model.
core.p: The **fetch-decode-execute cycle** (also called the **fetch-execute cycle**) is the continuous process by which the CPU runs a program. In the **fetch** stage the next instruction is copied from main memory (RAM) into the CPU. In the **decode** stage the CPU works out what the instruction means. In the **execute** stage the CPU carries it out, for example by adding two numbers, copying a value, or changing which instruction comes next. As soon as one instruction has been executed, the cycle begins again with the next one. A program is therefore run as a long chain of tiny cycles.

bullets: **PC**: holds the address of the **next** instruction to fetch; it is **incremented** each cycle.
**MAR**: holds the **address** of the memory location to be accessed (read or write).
**MDR**: holds the **contents** just fetched from, or about to be written to, memory.
**ACC**: holds the **result of ALU calculations** and is where running totals are built up.
**CIR** (not in the OCR list but common): holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed.
Registers are **inside the CPU** and are the **fastest** storage in the computer.
Remember by function: PC = **where next**, MAR = **where now**, MDR = **what is there**, ACC = **answer so far**.
core.h: The registers and what each one holds
core.p: **Registers** are tiny, extremely fast storage locations inside the CPU that hold the values the cycle is working with at that moment. OCR expects you to know four. The **Program Counter (PC)** holds the **address of the next instruction** to be fetched. The **Memory Address Register (MAR)** holds the **address of the memory location** that is about to be read from or written to. The **Memory Data Register (MDR)** holds the **data or instruction that has just been fetched** from memory or is about to be written to memory. The **Accumulator (ACC)** holds the **results of calculations** done by the ALU. Many textbooks also describe a **Current Instruction Register (CIR)** that holds the instruction while it is decoded.

bullets: **Address bus**: carries the **address** from MAR to memory (one direction: CPU to memory).
**Data bus**: carries the **instruction or data** between memory and MDR (both directions).
**Control bus**: carries **control signals** (for example a read signal) and timing/clock signals.
A wider **address bus** means more memory locations can be addressed; a wider **data bus** carries more bits at once.
Only the **MAR** puts an address on the address bus; only the **MDR** sends or receives data on the data bus.
The three buses work **together** on every memory access.
core.h: The buses used in the cycle
core.p: Whenever the CPU fetches from or writes to memory it uses the buses. The **address bus** carries the memory address (taken from the MAR) from the CPU to memory, and is one-way. The **data bus** carries the instruction or data back from memory to the MDR, and is two-way because data can also be written to memory. The **control bus** carries control signals such as **read**, **write** and timing signals from the control unit. Knowing which bus carries what lets you describe the fetch stage properly in an exam.

bullets: **Step 1**: The **address** in the **PC** is copied to the **MAR**.
**Step 2**: The address is sent along the **address bus** to RAM, and the **control unit** sends a **read** signal on the control bus.
**Step 3**: The instruction held at that address is sent along the **data bus** to the **MDR**.
**Step 4**: The **PC is incremented** so that it holds the address of the next instruction.
**Step 5**: The instruction is copied from the MDR to the **CIR** (or passed to the **control unit**) to be decoded.
The PC is incremented **during the fetch**, not at the end of the cycle; this matters for jump instructions.
**Model answer for 'describe fetch'**: address in PC copied to MAR; instruction at that address fetched from RAM into MDR; PC incremented.
core.h: The fetch stage step by step
core.p: The fetch stage copies the next instruction from RAM into the CPU. It starts with the **PC**, which holds the address of the next instruction. The address is **copied from the PC to the MAR**. The **control unit** then sends a **read** signal along the control bus, the address travels on the **address bus**, and the instruction stored at that location in RAM is sent along the **data bus** and placed in the **MDR**. At the same time the **PC is incremented by 1** so it points to the following instruction. The instruction is then passed on (to the CIR or directly to the control unit) ready to be decoded.

bullets: Normal running = **sequential execution**: addresses 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on.
The PC is increased by **1** (in the simplified GCSE model; real CPUs add the instruction length).
The PC **always holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched**, never the one being executed.
A **jump or branch** instruction replaces the value in the PC with a new address.
When the program is loaded to start, the PC is set to the address of the **first instruction**.
If the PC is not updated correctly, the same instruction would be fetched forever or the program would run in the wrong order.
core.p: The program counter must always point to the **next** instruction, not the current one. Because instructions are stored one after another at consecutive addresses, adding 1 to the PC means the next fetch will take the next instruction in the sequence. This is how a program normally runs in order, one instruction after another. Incrementing during the fetch also means that the PC is already ready if the current instruction is a jump, which can simply overwrite it.

bullets: Decoding is carried out by the **control unit**.
The instruction is split into the **opcode** (what to do) and the **operand** (what to do it to or where to find it).
The control unit works from the CPU's **instruction set**, which lists the operations the CPU understands.
The CU sends **control signals** to the ALU, registers, memory and buses.
No calculation happens yet: decode is about **understanding**, execute is about **doing**.
Mark-scheme wording: 'the instruction is decoded by the control unit'.
core.p: After the fetch, the instruction is just a binary pattern. In the **decode stage** the **control unit (CU)** interprets it, working out **which operation** is required and **what data or address** it refers to. Most machine code instructions have two parts: an **opcode** (the operation, for example ADD or LOAD) and an **operand** (the data or the address to use). Once decoded, the control unit knows what the rest of the CPU must do and it generates the **control signals** that make the right components act in the execute stage.

bullets: **Arithmetic/logic (ADD, AND, compare)**: the **ALU** does the operation; the result goes to the **ACC**.
**Load**: copy a value from a memory address into a register (address to MAR, data back through MDR).
**Store**: copy a value from a register into a memory address (address in MAR, value in MDR, write signal).
**Jump/branch**: the **PC** is set to a new address, so the next fetch comes from that place.
**Halt**: the program stops and the cycle ends.
Execute may take **several clock cycles**, depending on the instruction.
After execute the CPU goes **straight back to fetch**.
core.p: In the **execute stage** the instruction is carried out. What happens depends on the instruction. For an **arithmetic or logic** instruction the **ALU** performs the operation and the result is held in the **accumulator**. For a **load** instruction a value is read from memory into a register (the MAR gets the address and the MDR receives the data). For a **store** instruction a value is written from a register to memory. For a **jump** instruction the **PC is overwritten** with a new address. When execution is finished, the cycle returns to the fetch stage.

bullets: **CU**: decodes instructions and sends **control signals** to manage the cycle.
**CU** also controls the **timing** and the movement of data between CPU, memory and I/O.
**ALU**: carries out **arithmetic** and **logical** operations and comparisons.
**ACC**: stores the ALU's **result**, ready to be used or stored.
Decisions in programs (if statements) rely on the ALU **comparing** values.
**Cache and registers** keep needed values close so the ALU is not kept waiting.
core.h: The roles of the ALU and control unit
core.p: Two components do most of the work in the cycle. The **control unit** coordinates everything: it controls the flow of data inside the CPU, sends control signals, decodes instructions and uses the clock to keep everything in step. The **arithmetic logic unit (ALU)** performs the **calculations** (addition, subtraction and so on) and **logical comparisons** (AND, OR, NOT, and whether values are equal or larger) that the instructions demand. The ALU gets its inputs from registers and returns its answer to the accumulator.

bullets: **Fetch 1**: PC (0) copied to MAR; MDR receives LOAD 100; PC becomes 1.
**Execute 1**: address 100 is read; the value 7 goes via the MDR into the ACC. ACC = 7.
**Fetch 2**: PC (1) copied to MAR; MDR receives ADD 101; PC becomes 2.
**Execute 2**: the value 5 is read from address 101; the ALU adds 7 + 5; ACC = 12.
**Fetch 3**: PC (2) copied to MAR; MDR receives STORE 102; PC becomes 3.
**Execute 3**: the contents of the ACC (12) are written to address 102.
**Fetch 4**: HALT is fetched and the program stops. See the trace table in the diagrams.
core.h: Worked trace of a mini program
core.p: The best way to understand the cycle is to follow a small program. Suppose RAM holds: address 0 **LOAD 100**, address 1 **ADD 101**, address 2 **STORE 102**, address 3 **HALT**; address 100 holds 7 and address 101 holds 5. These are made-up instructions to show the idea; OCR does not set a particular instruction set. The program starts with PC = 0 and ACC = 0. Each fetch brings in an instruction and increments the PC; each execute does the job. After running, address 102 holds 12 because 7 + 5 = 12.

bullets: A **jump** replaces the PC value, so the **next instruction fetched is from the new address**.
A **conditional** jump depends on the result of an **ALU comparison**.
**Loops** are made by jumping back to an earlier address.
**Selection** is made by jumping over instructions that should not run.
Function/subroutine calls also change the PC (the CPU must remember where to return).
Because the PC was already incremented in the fetch, the jump simply **overwrites** it.
core.p: Not every program just runs in order. **Selection** (if statements) and **iteration** (loops) need the CPU to move to a different instruction. A **jump** (branch) instruction contains an address, and when it is executed that address is **copied into the PC**, overwriting the incremented value. The next fetch then takes the instruction from the new address. A **conditional jump** only does this if a comparison made by the ALU is true. This is how loops repeat and how decisions change the path through a program.

bullets: **Clock speed** (Hz): cycles per second; 1 GHz = 1 000 000 000 Hz.
One instruction can take **several clock cycles** (fetch, decode and execute each need time).
**Cache** reduces the time spent fetching because it is faster than RAM.
**Multiple cores**: each core has its own set of registers and runs its own cycle.
Instructions per second = **clock cycles per second ÷ clock cycles per instruction** (simplified).
Always tie answers back to the cycle: 'so more instructions are fetched, decoded and executed each second'.
core.p: The **clock** sends regular pulses that keep each step in time, and each pulse lets the CPU move on a little, so a higher **clock speed** means the cycle is repeated more times per second. **Cache** is very fast memory inside or close to the CPU that holds copies of frequently used instructions and data; if the next instruction is in cache the fetch is much quicker than fetching from RAM. **More cores** means more than one cycle can be performed at the same time, one per core. These explain why changing each factor changes how many instructions the CPU can process each second.

bullets: Use words like **copied**, **sent**, **held**, **incremented**, **decoded**, **executed**.
Put steps **in order**; use 'then', 'next', 'finally' to show sequence.
Always say which **register** holds which **item** (address or data).
Mention the **bus** if the question asks how it is transferred.
Check the number of marks: one clear point per mark.
If asked for the **purpose** of a register, give its function, not just its name.
core.p: Questions on the cycle reward **order**, **vocabulary** and **precision**. Start with the stage names and then give the detail in sequence, using the register names. Typical 4 mark question: 'Describe the fetch stage'. Typical 6 mark question: 'Describe how the CPU runs an instruction using the PC, MAR, MDR and ACC'. Write one idea per sentence, in order, and make each register's role clear. Avoid vague phrases like 'the CPU goes and gets the instruction' because they are not rewarded.

bullets: **Binary and data representation**: instructions and data are stored as binary patterns.
**Boolean logic**: the ALU performs AND, OR and NOT operations built from logic gates.
**Translators**: high-level code is converted to machine code instructions that are then fetched and executed.
**Memory and storage**: programs are loaded from secondary storage to RAM before the cycle can use them.
**Programming constructs**: if statements and loops depend on jump instructions.
**Performance**: clock speed, cache and cores change how fast the cycle runs.
**Embedded systems**: they also run the cycle, just for one dedicated program.
core.p: The cycle connects to many other parts of the course. **Binary** explains why instructions and data are numbers; **logic gates** explain how the ALU works; **translators** explain where machine code comes from; the **operating system** and **memory management** explain how programs are loaded into RAM so the PC can find them; **performance** factors explain why different CPUs complete more cycles per second. **Algorithms and programming** (loops and selection) are implemented through jump instructions changing the PC.

exam: **Name the stages (1 to 3 marks)**: 'Fetch, decode, execute', in that order. Give them in sequence.
**Describe the fetch stage (up to 4 marks)**: address in PC copied to MAR; address sent on address bus; instruction fetched from RAM along data bus into MDR; PC incremented.
**State the purpose of a register (1 mark each)**: PC next address; MAR address of location accessed; MDR data/instruction fetched or to be written; ACC result of calculation.
**Decode (1 to 2 marks)**: 'the control unit decodes the instruction (into opcode and operand) and sends control signals'.
**Execute (1 to 2 marks)**: say what happens for the instruction given: ALU calculates and result goes to ACC, or PC is overwritten for a jump.
**Trace questions**: copy the table carefully; remember the PC has already increased after fetch. Show each register's value.
**6 mark question**: describe each stage in order, naming registers and components, then link to repetition and speed. Write in clear steps.
**Calculations**: convert GHz to Hz first, then divide by clock cycles per instruction; give units (instructions per second).
Avoid 'it goes to the memory and gets it'; use register names and 'copied' or 'sent'.
Use the bus names correctly: address bus (address), data bus (data/instructions), control bus (signals).

mistakes.r: The PC holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched.
mistakes.w: The PC holds the instruction that is currently being run.

mistakes.r: The MAR holds the address of the memory location; the MDR holds the data or instruction.
The order is fetch, then decode, then execute, and then the cycle repeats.
mistakes.w: The order is decode, fetch, execute.

mistakes.r: The control unit decodes the instruction; the ALU does arithmetic and logic.
Instructions are fetched from RAM (or cache) after being loaded from storage.
mistakes.w: The CPU fetches instructions from the hard drive.

mistakes.r: The PC is incremented during the fetch stage, so it already holds the next address.
mistakes.w: The PC is increased at the end of the execute stage.

mistakes.r: Describe the transfer: address copied from PC to MAR, instruction fetched into MDR via the data bus.
mistakes.w: The CPU 'goes and gets' the instruction (no detail).

mistakes.r: The accumulator stores the results of ALU calculations.
A jump overwrites the PC with a new address so execution continues from there.
mistakes.w: A jump adds 1 to the PC.

summary: OCR J277 1.1 asks you to describe the fetch-decode-execute cycle: the CPU repeatedly fetches an instruction from RAM (PC to MAR, instruction into MDR, PC incremented), decodes it in the control unit, and executes it (often using the ALU and accumulator). It matters because it is the mechanism behind every program and it is tested with ordered descriptions and traces.

terms.d: The repeated process by which the CPU fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it and executes it.
The stage in which the next instruction is copied from main memory into the CPU.
The stage in which the control unit works out what the fetched instruction means.
The stage in which the CPU carries out the decoded instruction.
A register that holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched.
A register that holds the address of the memory location that is to be read from or written to.
A register that holds the data or instruction that has just been fetched from memory or is about to be written to memory.
A register that holds the results of calculations carried out by the ALU.
A register, used in many textbooks, that holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed.
The part of the CPU that decodes instructions and controls the flow of data and timing by sending control signals.
The part of the CPU that carries out arithmetic and logical operations and comparisons.
A very small, extremely fast storage location inside the CPU.
The set of wires that carries the address of a memory location from the CPU to memory.
The set of wires that carries data and instructions between the CPU and memory.
The set of wires that carries control signals, such as read and write, around the computer.
The two parts of an instruction: the opcode states the operation to perform and the operand is the data or address it acts on.
To increase a value by a fixed amount, usually 1, as the PC is increased in the fetch stage.
An instruction that changes the value in the PC so that the next instruction is fetched from a different address.

worked.ans: The address in the program counter is copied to the MAR. The address is sent on the address bus to RAM with a read signal. The instruction stored at that address is sent along the data bus into the MDR. The program counter is incremented so it holds the address of the next instruction.
worked.q: Describe the fetch stage of the fetch-decode-execute cycle. [4 marks]
steps: Mark 1: address of the next instruction in the PC is copied to the MAR.
Mark 2: the address is sent along the address bus and the control unit sends a read signal.
Mark 3: the instruction at that address is sent along the data bus from RAM to the MDR.
Mark 4: the PC is incremented to point to the next instruction.

worked.ans: PC = 2, MAR = 1, MDR = ADD 101; after execution ACC = 12.
worked.q: RAM holds: address 0 LOAD 100, address 1 ADD 101, address 2 STORE 102. Address 100 holds 7 and address 101 holds 5. After the second instruction has been fetched but not yet executed, give the values of the PC, the MAR and the MDR. After it has been executed, give the value of the ACC. [4 marks]
steps: The second instruction is at address 1, so the MAR holds 1 when it is fetched.
The MDR holds the instruction fetched: ADD 101.
The PC has already been incremented, so it holds 2 (the next instruction).
Executing ADD: ACC already holds 7 from the LOAD; 7 + 5 = 12.

worked.q: A CPU has a clock speed of 2.5 GHz. Each instruction takes 5 clock cycles. Calculate (a) the number of instructions processed per second and (b) the time to process 2 000 000 instructions. [4 marks]
